q6.answer: The server checks the header format (pat_ plus 32 characters), computes the SHA-256 of the presented token and looks up the api_tokens row by token_hash (unique index). The row is usable only if revoked_at IS NULL and expires_at > now() (database clock). Otherwise there is no row and the request gets the generic 401. Validity is never cached.

q7.answer: The auth lookup returns a database-computed stale flag (last_used_at IS NULL or older than 1 hour). Only when stale is true does the server run an UPDATE of last_used_at = now() after the response. The UPDATE repeats the stale condition in its WHERE clause, so concurrent requests produce one effective write, and a fresh token causes no write. That gives at most about one write per token per hour.

q8.answer: Nothing happens to the request. The update runs after the response is sent, so the API request still succeeds. The server logs the failure without the token, and last-used stays stale until the next stale request tries again.

q9.answer: Revoking sets revoked_at = now() on the api_tokens row in a single UPDATE. The row is not deleted. The list query filters on revoked_at IS NULL and expires_at > now(), so the revoked token disappears from the list. It also stops counting toward the limit of 10 and no longer blocks reuse of its name. The auth lookup rejects it on the very next request.

q10.answer: The UPDATE has WHERE id = ID AND user_id = session user AND revoked_at IS NULL. Another user's token, an unknown id and an already revoked token all affect 0 rows and return the same 404, with no state change. The 404 does not reveal whether the id exists for someone else.

q11.answer: The row was already committed with its hash, so it exists and counts toward the limit of 10, but the plaintext is gone and cannot be resent. The user sees it in the list with last used "Never", revokes it and creates a new one. Retrying with the same name returns 409 (name in use) until the old one is revoked.
